title: Building a Workbench With Only Hand Tools (No Power, No Excuses)
creator: Callum Price
description:
A full-size Roubo-style workbench built with nothing but hand saws, planes and chisels. It took eleven days and most of my patience.

Plans for this bench are in my shop: callumpricewoodworks.com/plans
Use code BENCH10 for 10% off any of my plans.

Timber: reclaimed beech from a local school gym floor.

sentences.t: Right, this pile of wood used to be the floor of a school gym, and in eleven days it's going to be a workbench.
And I'm doing the whole thing with hand tools, no table saw, no planer, nothing with a plug.
Mostly because I wanted to see if I could, and partly because my neighbours have complained about the noise.
So this is beech, and it's absolutely full of old nails and screw holes, which is the first problem.
I've gone over every board with a magnet, pulling out anything metal, because hitting a nail with a hand plane will ruin your week.
Found forty-one nails.
Missed one, as you'll see later.
Okay, the top.
I've glued up six boards into a slab about four inches thick, and now it needs to be flat.
Flat flat, not kind of flat.
So I'm using winding sticks, which are just two straight bits of wood, to see where the top is twisted.
Then I go across the grain with a big scrub plane to knock the high spots down.
This is about two full days of work, and my shoulders are not happy about it.
And there's the nail I missed.
You can hear it.
That's a big chunk out of my plane iron, so I'm going to have to grind that back before I can carry on.
Quick thing while I'm sharpening, because a lot of you asked last time.
I've drawn up full plans for this bench, with every measurement, a cut list, and step-by-step drawings for the joints.
They're in my little online shop, the link is in the description, and if you use the code BENCH10 you get ten percent off.
It's just me running it, no company, and honestly the plans are what let me spend eleven days making one video like this.
Okay, back to the bench.
Now the legs.
The legs join the top with a mortise and tenon, and the tenons go all the way through.
I'm chopping the mortises with a big chisel and a mallet, about an inch at a time.
The trick is to keep checking the sides with a square, because it is so easy to drift sideways and end up with a leg that leans.
For the stretchers, the bits that connect the legs at the bottom, I'm using drawbore joints.
That means the hole in the tenon is drilled slightly off from the hole in the mortise.
When you hammer the peg in, it pulls the joint tight, no glue, no clamps.
This is a really old technique and it still blows my mind every time.
Listen to that, it just goes thunk and it's done.
Day nine, assembly.
The top weighs something like eighty kilos, so I had to get my brother over to help me lift it onto the legs.
He wasn't thrilled.
But it dropped on perfectly, first time, and the whole thing doesn't wobble at all.
Finishing.
I'm keeping it simple, just a couple of coats of boiled linseed oil and some paste wax.
You don't want a workbench too slippery, otherwise everything slides around when you're planing.
And then the last job is boring the dog holes, so I can clamp things flat to the top.
So, eleven days, no power tools, one missed nail and one very annoyed brother.
Would I do it again?
Ask me in a month when my shoulders have recovered.
Next video, I'm building the leg vise for it, and that's going to involve a lot of threading by hand.
Cheers for watching.
